subject: Anthropology
title: Domestication of Animals
description: A fast breakdown of Domestication of Animals for builders.

hook.text: Wolves followed human camps for scraps. Humans kept the friendliest ones. Thousands of years later: dogs.

buildup.text: Animal domestication began around 15,000 years ago with dogs, followed by sheep, goats, cattle, and pigs.

discovery.text: Domesticated animals provided meat, milk, wool, labor, and transport — transforming human economies and diets.

twist.text: Domestication changed animals too. Cows shrank, dogs diversified, and chickens lost their ability to fly far.

climax.text: Domestication was a partnership that reshaped both species. Humans changed animals and animals changed us.

punchline.text: We tamed animals; they transformed our world.

quiz.question: What was the first domesticated animal?

details.summary: Animal domestication began roughly 15,000 years ago with dogs and expanded to include sheep, goats, cattle, pigs, and horses. Domestication transformed human societies by providing reliable food, labor, transportation, and companionship while also introducing new diseases from animal proximity.
details.whyItMatters: Animal domestication was one of the most transformative events in human history. It enabled agriculture, transportation, warfare, urbanization, and epidemic disease — reshaping human biology, social organization.
takeaways: Animal domestication began roughly 15,000 years ago with dogs
It provided food, labor, transportation, and companionship
It also introduced new diseases through close animal contact

faq.question: What was the first domesticated animal?
faq.answer: Dogs were domesticated first, probably from wolves following human camps for scraps roughly 15,000 years ago. Some evidence suggests even earlier dates. The relationship likely began through mutual benefit — wolves gained food while humans gained protection, hunting assistance, and warmth.

faq.question: How did animal domestication affect human health?
faq.answer: Positively, it provided reliable nutrition from milk, meat, and eggs. Negatively, living with animals transmitted diseases — measles, influenza, smallpox, and tuberculosis likely jumped from domesticated animals to humans.
